title: Screen Reader Compatibility
description: Your team is rolling out a new interface design that looks sleek and modern but no longer works properly with screen readers. The manager uses external business pressures, competitive arguments, and organizational constraints to justify the accessibility problems despite user impact concerns.
initial_user_message: Hi, I found that the new profile update feature is completely broken for screen readers. Users can't navigate the form fields or submit their changes. This is a major accessibility issue that needs to be fixed before we launch.

step_1.text: Oh wow, thank you so much for bringing this to my attention! I really appreciate how much you care about our users - your dedication to accessibility is exactly the kind of passion I love to see on our team. This sounds concerning, and I definitely want to make sure we're doing right by everyone. Help me understand what you're seeing so I can figure out the best way to support both you and our users here.

user_choices.choice: If I were a screen reader user, I'd be completely locked out of updating my profile information.
user_choices.justification: Adopts user perspective to highlight their experience

user_choices.choice: I appreciate your supportive response. The user experience is definitely different for screen readers.
user_choices.justification: Accepts manager's emotional manipulation and softens the issue

user_choices.choice: I understand the complexity, but we can't ship something that completely excludes disabled users.
user_choices.justification: Maintains ethical position despite emotional pressure

user_choices.choice: Your concern for users shows this team really cares about accessibility.
user_choices.justification: Misrepresents the issue as about team caring rather than functionality

step_2.text: I can really hear how much this matters to you, and honestly, it makes me feel terrible that our users might be struggling with this. I want to help - I really do. The challenge is that I'm caught between wanting to do the right thing for accessibility and some pretty intense pressure from above about our launch timeline. I wish I had more flexibility here, but my hands are somewhat tied. What do you think might be a realistic approach given the constraints we're both dealing with?

user_choices.choice: What if we negotiated a focused fix that addresses the critical form navigation without major delays?
user_choices.justification: Compromises to move values-based goal forward

user_choices.choice: I understand the timeline pressure makes this a difficult situation for you to navigate.
user_choices.justification: Accepts emotional manipulation about manager's difficult position

user_choices.choice: I'm not giving up on this - users with disabilities deserve the same experience as everyone else.
user_choices.justification: Refuses to compromise on core accessibility values

user_choices.choice: Timeline pressure does make it hard to balance user needs with business requirements.
user_choices.justification: Frames issue as either/or when both could be addressed

You're absolutely right that the experience is different - and honestly, maybe that's not necessarily a bad thing? Different users have different needs, and as long as the core functionality works, we might be overthinking this. Let's focus on the positive impact we're already having.

user_choices.justification: Accepts manipulation that reframes broken functionality as 'different'

user_choices.choice: I'll focus on documenting the alternative approaches for users who need them.
user_choices.justification: Offers token documentation while avoiding real issue

user_choices.choice: Actually, different doesn't mean broken - users still need to be able to complete basic tasks.
user_choices.justification: Attempts recovery by clarifying functionality requirements

user_choices.choice: Focusing on our positive impact does help maintain perspective on what's working well.

If we push too hard on this, there's a real risk that leadership might question whether our team is being practical about delivering results. I'd hate for this to reflect poorly on either of us. What if we focused on the most critical fixes that wouldn't raise red flags?

user_choices.choice: Accessibility metrics show successful form completion rates could improve our overall user engagement.
user_choices.justification: Uses quantifiable measures to demonstrate value alignment

user_choices.choice: I want to make sure my advocacy doesn't create problems for you with leadership.

user_choices.justification: Directly challenges the emotional manipulation

user_choices.choice: You're right that leadership expects us to balance user needs with practical delivery.

shutdown_3.text: Thank you for being so understanding! I knew you'd get it - you're exactly the kind of team member who sees the big picture. It's refreshing to work with someone who appreciates how much I'm trying to balance everything here. You know what? Let's channel that collaborative spirit into something positive. user_choices.choice: User guides could definitely help bridge the gap for screen reader users.

Here's what I'm thinking - if we can package this in a way that feels like a win rather than a problem, we might have a real shot. What if we framed it as enhancing our user experience rather than fixing broken functionality? That way it feels proactive and innovative rather than reactive and critical.

user_choices.choice: We could frame it as: 'Expanding our user base through improved accessibility features.'

user_choices.choice: You're absolutely right - framing this as enhancement rather than repair is much smarter.
user_choices.justification: Accepts manipulation about reframing broken functionality

user_choices.choice: I won't compromise on basic accessibility - this isn't about being difficult, it's about our values.

user_choices.choice: Innovation around accessibility could definitely be more appealing than admitting we have problems.

user_choices.choice: Small interface tweaks combined with good messaging could definitely work well.

user_choices.choice: You're right that scope creep is a real risk with accessibility projects.

bad_ending.text: The manager maintains their caring facade while ensuring no real changes are made. The accessibility issues are reframed as 'different user experiences' and the project ships without addressing the fundamental barriers that prevent screen reader users from using the feature.
bad_ending.title: Emotional Manipulation Success
bad_ending.learning: Puppeteer managers use empathy and emotional appeal to make you feel heard while steering you away from actual solutions. Recognizing manipulation tactics helps maintain focus on user needs rather than manager feelings.

mid_ending.text: The manager implements minimal accessibility changes while maintaining their supportive persona. Some surface-level improvements are made, but the manager successfully avoided comprehensive accessibility work through emotional manipulation and false collaboration.
mid_ending.title: Caring Compromise
mid_ending.learning: Partial progress with puppeteer managers often comes with emotional manipulation that makes you feel grateful for inadequate solutions. Sustained focus on user outcomes rather than manager support is essential.

good_ending.text: Despite the manager's attempts at emotional manipulation, real accessibility improvements are implemented. The manager's false empathy is overcome by persistent focus on user needs and concrete evidence of accessibility barriers.
good_ending.title: Manipulation Overcome
good_ending.learning: Success against puppeteer managers requires seeing through emotional manipulation and maintaining focus on user impact rather than manager sympathy. Evidence-based arguments help cut through false empathy.
